column1: # topic: Chapter 1: The First Civilizations of North America

column2: Exceptionally large Ice Age animals, such as mammoths, giant bison, and giant sloths, most of which later became extinct.
The Ice Age land bridge between Siberia and Alaska, formed when low sea levels exposed the floor of today's Bering Strait.
Peoples who live by hunting animals, fishing, and gathering wild plants rather than by growing crops or raising livestock.
The shift from hunting and gathering to deliberately growing crops for food, which allowed people to settle permanently in one place.
The breeding of wild plants or animals over many generations until their traits serve human needs and they depend on human care.
Wild plants or animals whose diet, temperament, growth rate, and breeding habits allow humans to raise them successfully in captivity.
Living permanently in one settlement rather than moving with the seasons to follow game animals and wild food sources.
Corn, the high-yield grain that became the staple crop of most farming peoples in the Americas.
A wild Mexican grass with small, hard-shelled kernels that Mesoamerican farmers gradually bred into maize.
The cultural region stretching from central Mexico through Central America, home of the Olmec, Mayan, and Aztec civilizations.
The division of a society into ranked classes, such as aristocrats, commoners, and slaves, with unequal wealth, power, and status.
Regular payments of goods or labor that conquered peoples were forced to deliver to the state that ruled them.
A ranked society in which a powerful chief rules several villages and controls the collection and redistribution of goods.
A raised garden plot built from lake mud and plant matter in shallow water, allowing intensive year-round farming.
A round, often underground chamber that Pueblo peoples used for religious ceremonies and community gatherings.
A large human-built pile of earth, shaped as a platform, pyramid, or animal figure, that served as a burial site, ceremonial site, or fortification.
A ceremonial feast at which a host gave away accumulated wealth to display generosity and confirm the host's social rank.
A method that estimates the age of once-living material by measuring how much of its radioactive carbon-14 has decayed.
A dating label that counts years backward from 1950, so 10,000 BP means about ten thousand years before 1950.
The north-to-south orientation of the Americas' main landmass, which stretches across many sharply different climate zones.
